summary: NETCONF servers can have default values for settings the client never set. This standards-track document defines a capability that tells how the server handles those defaults when reporting configuration. Clients can then ask for defaults to be shown or hidden in consistent ways.

plainLanguage.summary: If you never pick a setting, the device uses a default. This lets you say whether you want to see those untouched defaults in a report.

questions: how does netconf report default values

subtitle: A NETCONF capability that tells clients how a server treats default values and lets them choose whether to see them.

tldr.problem: NETCONF servers handle default values in different ways. Some hide them, some always show them, and the difference changes both what a client reads back and whether create and delete operations succeed.
tldr.mechanism: A server advertises one of three basic modes (report-all, trim or explicit) in a capability URI. A new with-defaults parameter on get, get-config and copy-config lets the client ask for a particular reporting mode, including a tagged one.
tldr.outcome: Clients can learn exactly how a server handles defaults and can ask for the complete set of values when they need it. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6243 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Default Data Problem
sections.content:
Part of a device's configuration may never be set by the NETCONF client. Instead a default value from the data model is used. Often the client already knows these defaults, for example from a document describing the data models, so the server does not need to send them.

Sometimes the client does need them. The RFC lists several cases: a management application may want a single, definitive and complete set of configuration values, documentation about defaults can be unreliable or unavailable, some applications cannot parse formal data models, and human users may want to read the data without consulting documentation. Servers differ, and the differences affect two things: what gets returned on retrieval, and whether create and delete operations succeed, since those depend on whether a node currently exists.
sections.plainLanguage: When a toy comes with settings already chosen, you may or may not want a list that shows them. This document gives you a way to ask for the list or skip it.

sections.title: Default Data and Explicitly Set Data
sections.content:
Schema default data is data the data model schema marks as default, used whenever the client or other management user does not provide a value. Whether it is stored in a datastore depends on the server's basic mode. Default data is conceptual data holding a default value; it is not kept in a datastore. A node that is missing from the datastore while a schema default is in use counts as a default data node.

Explicitly set data is data set to any value by a client or other management application through an explicit operation, including a value equal to the schema default. Any value set by the server that is not the schema default is also explicitly set.
sections.plainLanguage: A default is the pencil case that came pre-filled. Explicitly set data is anything you put in yourself, even if you picked the very same pencil.

sections.title: The Three Basic Modes
sections.content:
Rather than force one strategy, the RFC lets a server pick one of three basic modes and advertise it. A server MUST select exactly one. Clients are expected to handle all three.

  • report-all: no node is considered default data, even schema defaults. All nodes are reported. The server treats every node as existing, so create of a node holding its default fails with data-exists, and delete succeeds even though the server immediately restores the default.
  • trim: any node set to its schema default is default data and is not reported. Setting a node to its default succeeds but the node is not saved. create succeeds, and delete of a missing node that has a schema default fails with data-missing.
  • explicit: any node not explicitly set is default data. Nodes explicitly set by the client are reported even if they equal the default. create fails with data-exists if the client set the node to its default and succeeds if the server did; delete is the mirror image, succeeding for client-set nodes and failing with data-missing for server-set ones.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of note-takers. One writes down everything, one skips anything that is just the usual, and one writes down only what you personally asked for.

sections.title: Asking for a Reporting Mode
sections.content:
The new <with-defaults> parameter takes one of four values. A server MUST accept the values for the modes it supports.

  • report-all: report all nodes, including those the server treats as default.
  • trim: do not report nodes holding the schema default, including non-configuration nodes.
  • explicit: report nodes the client set to the default, do not report nodes the server would conceptually default, and report non-configuration nodes holding the default.
  • report-all-tagged: like report-all, but each node the server considers default data carries a default XML attribute.

Tagged mode lets an application see in a single retrieval which nodes are default. A server supporting it MUST also accept the default attribute in configuration input to <edit-config> or <copy-config>. Setting it to true or 1 asks for the node to be returned to its default, and the node's value MUST equal the schema default or the server returns an invalid-value error. The attribute uses the XSD boolean type, and implementations MUST support both the 0/false and 1/true forms.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameter is a switch on the report. You can show everything, hide the usual stuff, show only what you set, or show everything with a sticker on the usual stuff.

sections.title: The With-defaults Capability
sections.content:
A server advertises :with-defaults with the identifier urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:with-defaults:1.0. The identifier MUST carry a basic-mode parameter with the value report-all, trim or explicit. It MAY carry an also-supported parameter, a comma-separated list of other modes the server will accept. The capability has no dependencies, adds no new operations, and has no interactions with other capabilities.

The server MUST support the YANG module ietf-netconf-with-defaults for its basic mode and SHOULD support it for report-all or report-all-tagged. That module adds the with-defaults leaf to get, get-config and copy-config. A server MUST also advertise a YANG module capability URI as RFC 6020 requires. The capability covers both configuration and state data, and default sending is controlled per operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The device holds up a card that says which note-taker it is and which other styles it can also do, so you know what to ask for.

sections.title: Effects on Existing Operations
sections.content:
If <with-defaults> is absent, the server follows its basic mode. If the value is one the server does not support, it MUST return an invalid-value error. For get and get-config, defaults filtering is conceptually done before the <filter> parameter, so a filter sees all nodes under report-all.

copy-config is affected only when the target is given by <url>. When the target is a configuration datastore (running, candidate or startup), the server uses its basic mode and silently ignores the parameter. In edit-config, only the create and delete operations are affected by the basic mode. If a client sets a node to its default, the server accepts it when valid, then keeps or discards it by basic mode; only trim discards. Other operations that return configuration data SHOULD follow the same rules and say so in their own documentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch only changes what is printed in the report. The things stored on the device stay the same.

sections.title: Security and Registrations
sections.content:
The document says it does not introduce new or increased security risks. The capability gives clients control over retrieval of default data from a datastore, and the security considerations of RFC 6241 apply.

IANA registers the capability URN, two XML namespace URNs (urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:default:1.0 and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-netconf-with-defaults) and the YANG module name ietf-netconf-with-defaults with prefix ncwd. The appendix gives a terse example YANG module and example <with-defaults> requests for each mode; the example module is not required for conformance.
sections.plainLanguage: It only changes what is shown in a report, so it does not add new ways to break in.
